title: Star Ruler
text: Woa this one is a bit hard to review. It's an old game from an old distant galaxy in the olden times... Fast review: If it's 10$ or less, you can buy it, over that go buy starforce 2 instead! Much better in everyway!!! Now for the detailed review: - Space strategy 4x game realtime with pause and adjustable speed. Colonize planets, develop them, build ships, conquer - There ain't much graphics in this game. An old windows xp can run this game fine. Ship battle are kinda 2D boring affair. - There is far too much bass in the background music! I had to turn it off after a few minutes, i was THAT annoyed by it. - The gui is unpolished. It's not buggy, but it's not intuitive. It takes quite a while to find out where everything is and how it works. Because it's not a big AAA game, there ain't much information either in forums or elsewhere. It's pretty sparse. But on the other hand, if you stick with it, the learning curve is not that bad. Nothing compared to Distant Universe for example. - The ship design is unique compared to any game i've played. Designing a dreadnought or a cruiser is the same, only the amount of armor and the hull choice seems to decide what amount of HP the ship has, but they both will have the same amount of components. A bit dull if you ask me. Clunky too. But, god it's complicated at first with something like 20 stats that you can affect with the components you include. Example: Amount of ammo your ship has, the amount he will spend by second, the amount of fuel, amount of fuel spent by second, amount of energy generated and on and on. I think it's a bit too much detail, but you can design your ship to your heart content! Also, all ships pretty much looks the same, only difference is size (which you can also set. If you want a fighter bigger looking than your dreadnought, you can do that too!). - The research graph is interesting and kinda fun. I like it. It's also one of the few part of the game that is intuitive and easy to understand and use. - The zoom and map movement is pretty horrible. It made me think of the first 3D game i've ever played where they had not yet mastered how to move the camera in 3D. Haven't found a good way yet to move around my empire except by planet name. And the funny part is that the game may look like 3D, but you actually move only in 2D. HAHAHA! - The amount of ships you are going to lose because of them reaching empty fuel is pretty crazy. You need tankers everywhere and in large numbers. Yeah if a ship or fighter reach zero fuel, they die and can't be 'revived' except maybe with boarding ships. On the other hand, there are no cash and no ship maintenance in this game. So if you want a fleet with 1 million ships, you can go ahead and do it. You seem to only be limited by the amount of ore that is on planets and asteroids. - You can automate each ship with pretty detailed orders, but you can also shoot yourself in the foot repeatedly with a bad automated order. It does not always act like you think it does. And there are no explaination anywhere about them. So go go experiment. - Everything in the game will improve with the appropriate tek researched. Every building on planets, every component on a ship including armor and hull. There are a lot of research fields. - You can retrofit ships as long as you kept the same design name. For example, 'Carrier' blueprint. If you changed the name, then it is not considered the same class of ship and no retrofit for you. So you keep the starting design from start to end game. Does not matter that you completely change a ship vocation and components, as long as the design name is the same you can retrofit it. - You will make millions of ships. Eventually, you won't even bother and you will put your planets on repeat order so they crank out the same ships forever. And you send them attacking the frontier. You can have a biiiiiiiig empire. A bit hard to manage properly thought. - They kept the physics in the game as newtoninan as possible with even ship mass and thruster power. Depending on mass, a ship can take awhile before changing speed or even direction! It sure is pretty realistic, but i don't think it makes for very fun battles. The amount of errors you will make in your designs before you get them just right is going to be huge. - I've looked at the starforce 2 game and it seemed much better than this one. They kept the same concept, but graphics are loads better, the gui too is a lot more friendly with nice icons that do what they look like, spying and improved diplomacy to do dirty trics and the design of ships seems much more interesting and fun. Also, unlimited galaxy that you can generate! You decide the shape of the map and how many stars there is and they generate it for you! You are only limited by the speed of your computer! So you can 'in theory' generate a billion star map! It won't play well but you can do it! - Diplomacy is pretty bare bone and pointless. Enemy ai don't seem too challenging either after you master the game. Everything looks a bit bland. Once you played one game to completion, you don't really want to play another one.

title: StarBreak
text: I wish Steam had a yellow 'meh' rating. Starbreak has some great sidescrolling shooter/rpg elements, but like all perma death games it leads you to rage quitting, a lot. The XP system is more your typical F2P progression system where levels are used to 'unlock' access to different playable characters, all of which have their own unique purpose and playstyle but sadly all of which suck compared to the starting class. Like most perma death games you can pick up random drops which upgrade your stats minorly like a stat point, until death. You can also loot gear to improve your character, the combination of the two (Stats+Gear) More or less equals your "level". That is to say levels seem to be classified into 5 difficulties, Easy, medium, hard, very hard and extreme. While there are different playable levels of the same difficulty, all difficulties drop the same tier stat upgrades and gear. However, each playable level has a different boss, each boss has their own achievement for beating them. The Perma death structure isn't so bad, yeah it causes rage quitting because you lose stuff that was hard to find, almost always you die in the most lame way possible, the game usual pulls one of those ridiculous "all the games rules are broken" moves where you get hit and it somehow becomes an endless combo till you die. One of my primary issues is that Starbreak is ALSO F2P. You see Starbreak has 2 different currencies, your basic and your paid premium. First off as far as my experience goes, money has no functional affect on gameplay, all monetarily obtainable items are cosmetic or storage based. The basic "EC" is something you get through due course of the game, but the premium "UC" is only purchasable, so when you die you lose the item and the money forever. Seems pretty hanky to me. Overall Starbreak is a shallow but enjoyable side scrolling shooter with rpg elements. Well executed but with Perma death as the games base mechanic it can't offer very deep gameplay because of the failure penalty. In combination with paid for content though that also gets deleted when you die I give it a 'meh'. Perma death is rather annoying anyway, it forces shallow investment mechanics into a game because no one wants to spend weeks working on a character just to get it deleted anyway, so perma death games have to offer a rapid and simple 'leveling' system of some sort to compensate. This makes it a great game though for a short gaming session just to kill some time. No story. No complicated controls or mechanics to learn. Just a straight old school arcade style side scolling shooter. 5/10 Final Note: If you're the type that hates being cheated, don't EVER play the level "The Strands". 50% of the time you'll start the level being hit by an enemy which will kick you into insta death, you'll literally spawn into the level already defeated and just get to see your character fall into the endless void and all your hard work instantly deleted.

title: StarBreak
text: Before I begin: Don't go down-voting this review because you hate seeing your favorite game getting criticism. Instead, actually read through this review, and take into consideration the things I have to say, as much of what is here could be considered a legitimate reason for viewing a game so negatively. Many issues I will be pointing out here have also been pointed out by not just myself, but others on both sides of the 'aisle'. All I ask is that you allow a guy a moment to offer his opinion. Seeing as I apparently earned the ire of a few people for being 'negative about a perfect game', I'm rewriting this review to give more people insight into why I cannot recommend this game. I even TRIED to enjoy it, TRIED to play it and see the good in it, even after writing this the first time. As you can plainly see: Not much has changed, and I've only come away from it with more to focus on. First of all: I still stand by the feeling that this has the 'potential' to be a great game with some pretty interesting mechanics. However, the mechanics are also what make this such a difficult game for me (and others) to like and enjoy. The gameplay is fun when you're on a roll, when you're blasting through enemy after enemy, finding really good gear to use, and just nailing those difficult jumps and attacks when it really matters. But the progression and combat mechanics can also make all of that work you've put into leveling damn-near useless, no matter how good you get. When you die, you lose everything, including gear and stats. When you enter a new shell, you start back at square 1: bare bones stats, the most basic of weapons, no body or mobility gear, and not one thing to show for the amount of work you put into playing, except for a little pocket change and a tiny handful of experience points. Even then, it's not worth the trouble, as money is currently useless, and your level only dictates which shells you can use. When out on the field, you pick up stat boosts to enhance your shell's abilities, which is all fine and dandy, as a couple extra HP can mean the difference between life and death. As you collect these stats, you will sometimes find that you max out an ability. This means that you've just maxed out one ability needed for the increase of your shell's MK level! Awesome! But, like I said: You die, you lose it all, and you have to do it all again. The only way to keep those stats is to stay alive through the entire dungeon. What doesn't help is that you have to collect MK II upgrades from harder dungeons, which means...You guessed it. You're gonna lose all that work, and lose that shiny MK II rating. It's not fun, it's not an enjoyable feature, and the only players who claim to see this as enjoyable are the 'hardcore' players, or those who believe the risk-reward system is 'perfect'. Not everyone is a masochist. If you want to save those stats, plus the gear you managed to scrape up off the ground in a dungeon, you have the choice to purchase the game's premium currency, which can then be used to unlock a shell storage container, allowing you to switch out to another shell when you want to. Buying the currency is the only way to get these handy dandy containers, as, even if you were given the option, you'll almost never be likely to have the cash on-hand to pay for it, seeing as dungeons pay you in literal pocket change. Oh yeah, you can even buy cosmetics with that same premium currency! But, like every other item in the game, it can be rendered useless, not to mention non-existent, the moment you die. In other words, you're wasting your time and money on something that doesn't even help you. People say it only costs you a few cents, but the amount really starts to add up, as you grab those same items and try a dungeon again. And again. And again. And again. It starts to add up very quickly. You may be wondering, though: 'Just how easy would it be to die in this game? It all looks easy!' Trust me. You'll die easily. SO easily, in fact, that you can likely attribute your death to either sluggish framerate, poor terrain generation, enemy placement, or a ridiculous combo of any and all of those things. Or you can attribute it to the often-insane number of players on-screen, which makes jumping and fighting nearly impossible in some situations, and it limits the amount of points you get when you die. Of course, you COULD run a dungeon solo. Wait wherever you spawned in at, give everyone a few minutes to die off or move on, and then you have all of those respawned monsters and a few treasures waiting for you. Just don't expect it to amount to much. Not only will you be fighting a ton of alien creatures looking to strip away all of those shiny boosts and pieces of gear you've picked up, you'll be fighting the controls as well. If you're using a controller, aiming is VERY clunky, not to mention very frustrating, as it's tied directly to your movement stick (left stick by default, or d-pad). You can only fire left or right, and then diagonally in between those directions. That's it. No shooting straight up or down. There's no precision shooting, and there's little garuntee you'll hit that enemy coming at you at an odd angle, as you have to find that sweet spot to make your shell fire in an upward direction. Controller users also have to wrestle with the VERY unusual right-stick special. Flick your right analog stick up, down, left or right, and you fire off a special skill. It's a pain trying to use that in the middle of a boss battle, especially when you try to quickly go back to your default primary and secondary fire buttons (B and X on Xbox controllers), and more so when you're trying to out-manuever both the boss AND it's minions (wo spawn in so frequently that you'll likely die in a pit of the blasted things). If you enjoy platforming games, or maybe just enjoy being put through hell for a handful of XP and credits that will do you very little, sure, this game is fun. But for others, myself included, this game just isn't fun. Fighting controls, fighting framerate issues, fighting BS terrain generation and enemy spawning, fighting the game's mechanics...None of that is fun, nor is it worth spending time trying to adjust to it. And there you have it. My reasons for not enjoying this game, and for not recommending it.

title: StarMade
text: If Minecraft is a sandbox, StarMade is the beach. And instead of getting a shovel, you're given a bulldozer. The way the weapon system works is great - if this were in minecraft, it'd be like strapping 4 bows to your arms, but instead of arrows you shoot pickaxes to mine faster. And do you like that epic mansion you built in singleplayer? Why not save the blueprint and rebuild it in multiplayer? All you need are the resources. AMAZING. What's more, the game is free. FREE. Go and try it out, then pay for the game anyway because it's damn fun. THESE DEVS CARE. Lots of updates, great community and massive potential. The game has a lot of great things in it, the core mechanics are solid and lots of different elements. Let's review some of the common comments: Great multiplayer - valid (this game is built for sharing with friends or strangers) Boring single player - mixed (there's not much "to do" other than fight pirates, build spaceships and mine resources. There wasn't much to do in Minecraft in Beta either. Quests are coming. Bugs - invalid (the game is free, try it first, and yeah it's an alpha) Real talk: you'll probably never build anything epic. You want to build the Enterprise? You won't. But you CAN download the blueprint. My only warning is that the game isn't optimised yet, and there are lag spikes even on recommended system requirements. Memory leaks are common in alphas and so I'm ok with this. Some funny bugs though, a trade guild convoy of about 5 ships crashed into a planet and was stuck. Dropped fps to about 1-5fps, practically unplayable, but also hilarious. Would lag again.

title: StarMade
text: I started off loving Starmade...then we broke up. Now I spend time thinking about maybe giving it a another shot. I got into the game just after the big graphical re-boot having played Minecraft for years and checking out every voxel based, procedurally generated game I could find. I trolled Greenlight and found many wanna be contenders but Starmade impressed me with it's vision of what it wants to be. Like any relationship we fall in love with what could be, an ideal, sometimes a projection we place onto the other. I am love with what Starmade is trying to be, but has not yet become. I lost interest for awhile when the docking update changed how turrets and ships dock. I was having a blast using the quirky old system to make a wide range of ships. The new system looks great and will solve many foibles and allow for a great variety of new designs. Just like with the Minecraft updates I got to enjoy a new game play each time Notch added something. Starmade is developing much the same way but because of it's own ambition each major update is quite disruptive. I have seen other early access wallow aimlessly, become abandoned or run off the rails in development. Starmade is doing none of these things. The danger, as I see it, is that Starmade may have trouble fulfilling it's grand ambitions. Yes this game has a learning curve and I had fun riding that curve. This is the gold-standard for a complex game. If the learning is fun; success, if it is tedious; go play a game more suited to your short attention-span. A simple game is easy to learn and may become boring. A game with depth and possibilities is going take time to master but will remain engaging. In it's current state (shipyards just released) Starmade is a very solid, playable early access game. There is a smattering of enemies to keep you improving your ship designs. There is no story arc yet but the ship-building is very polished. The Devs have built a proper foundation for an amazing game. It remains to be seen if they can build an engaging experience onto their ground-breaking mechanics while maintaining balance. Look elsewhere for the hate, I'm going to tell you what I love. >Design matters. Where you put modules and how you protect your ship will really make a difference. Lots of room for tactics, countermeasures and cool systems. My first death in the game was a suicide. I designed anti-personnel pulsers in the airlock. Two passes and you are still ok, the third pass: you're dead. (You can come in, look around and leave safely or... linger and die.) I died testing the system and laughed my♥♥♥♥♥off. >If you can dream it up you can build it. The first major ship I built was a salvage craft. I designed it to rescue shipwrecks. It was big and turned like a pig but fast and survivable. (I used it for daring rescue of a huge ship that got cored by pirates. It was an epic mission that left massive chucks missing from the old Flat-top but both vessels made it home intact. WooHoo) One of my favorites is the Tholian Enervater: a spider-themed hunter-killer. By design this craft can pursue a small fighter, slow it down using (web) multiple tractor beams (locking it in the crosshairs), rob it of power using (venom) an electro-mcGuffin ray and finally kill it. The theme of the spider worked both visually and tactically. Very Cool, good job Devs. I decided to make a Whale-ship that could swallow a pirate-craft whole and then eat it. It worked just as I had hoped. (Unfortunately collisions are unavoidable) I have stealth designs, a 'Tuttle-craft' for repairs, a surveyer/scout, a carrier/salvager, a mining ship with a huge beam.  = ]  Racing has just been introduced so now 'Tuning' will be a part of designing an efficient racer. > Hey, it's fun to fly too. Never mind the awesome build mode with simple and powerful symmetry & mirroring to reduce keystrokes... this is a very good space cockpit interface. Starmade features a huge number of elements introduced by previous space games but incorporates them well, often getting better results than its predecessors. It may not have the graphical grandeur of Klingon Academy but the systems controls are simple and easy to use in combat. After narrowly escaping from battle and badly damaged, I was able to reconfigure my systems and piece two non-functional weapons into one cobbled together mess of a gun (without going into build-mode). As I limped home I felt like Scotty, under an instrument panel with sparks flying, griping to the ham fisted captain who got us into this mess in the first place (oh, wait...that's me). Dog fighting is still a bit slow and not very dynamic with the current AI. I hope for more variation in their tactics besides "Send more guys".  Multiplayer servers often have custom pirates so there is lots of room for variety. >Potential. There's that dirty word again. With human crews for opponents in a more populated (by NPCs) world this game could be epic on a level beyond the average tired space-shooter game. It already has nailed the galactic map, shop-economy, building, flight control, and optimization. Read the developer's blog (Bench) to get a look at what is to come. The game updates every couple of weeks with new features, bug fixes and optimizations. >Powerful logic-driven systems. Think wireless redstone only more stable. Weapons with aux effects, electronic countermeasures and transporters. Shipyards to generate virtual designs and a BluePrint for your builds to save, share, upload, download & modify, all seamlessly. >Friendliest PvP I have ever seen in a game. >This game is better and more polished in it's Alpha state than many 'finished' releases I have bought. >Going into 2016 there has been a cargo and thruster update offering realistic, mass based acceleration and more thruster dynamics with user customizable settings. Fleets are set to add another dimension to the Meta-game. Slabs are expanding build-potential. For the earth bound crowd who complain that game is broken: try to find it in your imagination that this game is still in the chrysalis phase. The grub's body is utterly dissolved in the cocoon before it can be reborn into a butterfly. Early access is just that... if you don't get that stop bothering the developers and go play something with Zombies. For the Developers: Schine on.

title: SteamWorld Heist
text: SteamWorld Heist is a side scrolling, turn-based, tactical game where you're the commander of a group of space pirates drawn into unavoidable conflict against the Empire while performing routine heists. Although the game is in side-scrolling 2D, it encompasses the familiar genre staples such as a cover system and terrain variability while displaying some of its own mechanics such as bullet ricochet which add some depth to the simplified systems. While the game delivers an entertaining journey and tense combat, it suffers from a lacklustre story and somewhat repetitive mission structure in the latter half. + Dialogue and interactions between characters is really enjoyable as characters often share their entertaining back-stories with you after missions. + Combat is extremely well done, I've heard it compared to a simplified mix of XCOM/Worms. + Bullet ricochet is highly enjoyable as you can kill enemies hiding behind cover by ricocheting bullets in the blind spots where there is no cover. Getting unassisted ricocheted kills feel extremely  satisfying. + A lot of effort was placed into the audio and visual aspects of the game and it shows as the game oozes polish from every nook and cranny. + There's no grind for what amounts for a tactical game and that's surprising for me. Lower skilled characters can be carried and get essential 2 bars if they survived the mission easily bringing them up to the rest of the squad. + There's no reliance on RNG during the combat it's all skill. If you missed shot, YOU missed the shot as have full control of where you aim. If a character is out in the open then the chances of receiving damage is 90-100% and it was fully based on YOUR decision. + Combat while not difficult is often times tense under certain situations depending on your difficulty. + The difficulty curve is rather smooth. I played on Experienced and even though I got wiped on a few missions, it wasn't difficult to complete the game. + A unique-ish loot system that's literally all of the items found lying on the floor in missions plus the epic swag bonus which is often placed in a mildly inconvenient room forcing you to explore all rooms. Don't feel like managing your small inventory to store mission loot rewards, fine, simply go for the epic swag and leave all other items alone. - Story is kind of lacklustre and forgettable. - You can't equip weapons/items outside of missions. - Missions are too repetitive, you're often stuck doing the same things mission in, mission out and while enjoyable it does get tiresome. - Limited inventory results in management feeling extremely tedious as you're given generous amounts of loot as reward for completing missions. - Aborting missions cost 50% of your current money/water. Why is this a thing, there were times where I accidentally retried missions I'd completed instead of selecting the next mission and I had to slug through it again because I'd be penalised for nothing. - The game feels a bit too long and drawn out, almost like if it was padded with unnecessary content e.g. the 1 character missions. - There are times where the enemy AI is too accurate. This is clearly evident during the boss battle against the Queen. The general's bullet will ricochet a number of times and the result is a perfect shot no matter what. I've had this happen to me a lot during that battle to the point that it's unfair and too perfect. - Battles can become drawn out as result of the alert system which spawns a number of enemies of increasing difficulty when the counter has elapsed. I get why this is here but boy does it get annoying. +/- Hats...why are they a thing? They serve literally no purpose, no added stat benefit or complexity. +/- Loot is kind of boring as it simply boils down to +1 this or -1 that. +/- There are no unique group passive synergies when in combat other than the captain's Inspire ability. I feel like this is a missed opportunity seeing as how simplified the game is, this could've added some much needed depth and nuance to the combat. SteamWorld Heist is an overall enjoyable experience despite its shortcomings and is well worth the recommendation. The combat is tense, the dialogue is well written, the strategy and tactical mechanics while simple are extremely accessible and all of this results in a very entertaining package.

text: I did begin to enjoy the game more towards the end of it, however, I don’t think I can fully recommend the experience.  Gameplay feels slow, and that feels like a weird thing to say about a strategy game. The tedium of watching enemies and characters move around and climb ladders without a fast forward button wore me out after a while. This also made battles draw on forever, especially if it was an area you were re-attempting for grinding.  Early on in the game I made the mistake of starting on a higher difficulty. Tougher levels on this difficulty felt near impossible without only putting my best foot forward, leaving me to abandon lower leveled teammates who never got any xp for dying near the end. I surprisingly found myself grinding for a few levels between boss fights, a frustrating task given that battles move slow and that dead teammates and failed missions give you no xp.  Strategy in the game seems straightforward, and this becomes even more apparent on easier difficulties. It mostly feels like there’s only one viable response for most scenarios. Put in the same circumstance in a level, I would probably expect myself to always react the same way. However, on harder difficulties, if you have to improvise, you’ll probably lose a teammate. Once you get an ‘A -team’ together, there’s no point in attempting to train other teammates and without their later abilities, a lot of teammates feel identical.  After a few disheartening failures on the first boss, and being in no mood to replay old levels, I turned the difficulty down and then, before the 2nd boss, had to turn the difficulty down once more. From this point, I was just interested in getting the game off my list and, with the help of a completionist drive, blazed to the end of the game on casual mode.  The final area is not only the coolest one but contains the best weapons and, by this point, your A-team should have a whole onslaught of tools and abilities unlocked that makes gameplay feel more varied from battle to battle.   On the brighter side of things, I suppose I ended up enjoying Steamworld Heist by the end of the game. The general view of this game seems to be pretty positive and it does have a decent soundtrack plus the artstyle/world is charming.  Perhaps if I had played it on casual mode from the beginning I would’ve been able to recommend it, but simply based off of my experience, I wouldn’t suggest it to a friend.     Outline: Feels like a waste of time Slow AF movement Deaths have no XP - failing late into a boss battle means you’ve wasted 10 minutes and have to go back and grid If you play on higher difficulties - not really about skill, more about weapons and trying Struggled with anything beyond regular mode I did end up playing to the end: Switched off Experienced (assume this meant I’ve played games before) and a breezed through the last world Dialog is pointless, skipped all of it

title: SteamWorld Heist
text: The unique gameplay of turn based action worked pretty well.  It takes a bit of getting used to, but it works.  In terms of the style, the space western theme is pretty cool, as are the graphics, music, characters, and humor of the game. It's too bad that there weren't more of the larger levels where you can use four characters though.  Most levels you can only use two or three characters, but I think those are the parts of the game that really stood out, and there's too few of them. But overall, if you are into the turn based action gameplay thing, its pretty great.

title: SteamWorld Heist
text: As excellent as a 2D turn-based strategy action game can be. Worms-like combat in a single player story setting. You unlock different characters as you advance through the game. Some use pistols and get bonuses if they hit enemies from the back, some are snipers and can ricochet bullets off walls to get headshots or hit enemies that are behind cover, some use explosives for area damage, some have more health and deal more melee damage some use close range weapons. Then you can level them up and gear them as you like to create a party fit for your play style. You also find hats which are purely cosmetic, but it's kind of addicting to try and find them or shoot them off of enemies' heads and pick them up for yourself. The level design is very clever, letting you approach most situations in multiple ways... except on a few occasions near the end of the game. I especially found using snipers and killing enemies with crazy trickshots using the curves and walls in the level. It's a great game just like the first Steamworld game even though they have very little in common, mainly the aesthetics. Also recommend the Outsider DLC which includes a unique character and some new levels.
